core and rim mica analyses, thereby indicating a lack of significant retrograde overprint.
In order to better link mineral chemistry with microtextures, we have performed new
scanning electron microscope (SEM) analysis of peak burial minerals (phengite and
glaucophane), both within matrix and micro-shear zones, and all the compositional profiles show a
strikingly flat pattern across the studied crystals (see Figure R5). We decided to undertake
SEM analyses because the interaction volume is much smaller (~10 µm3) than for the
EPMA (~100 µm3), enabling a higher-resolution detection of potential retrogressive
imprints on the crystal rims. Even though the values of absolute concentration may not
be as accurate as those of the EPMA, the sensitivity of the instrument enables the
identification of fine compositional changes, if any. The absence of systematic zoning
trends (in particular towards crystal rims) confirms that retrogression did not affect the
studied crystals in their respective microstructural position. We can therefore safely
discard this possibility and confirm that the mechanical processes proposed in our study
did occur at peak burial conditions. The corresponding addition has been incorporated
into the manuscript at Line 188, and Figure R5 has been included as Supplementary
Fig. S7.

The measured mica isopleths are stable in most of the pseudosection calculated in
Figure 4b, and according to Fig. 4a, there are different generations of white mica. So,
why not using these generations to reconstruct a PT path appropriately?
Response: We kindly disagree with this statement. The mica compositions are
remarkably clustered in the 45-60% celadonite joint (Fig.4a is strongly zoomed in,
which gives a visual impression of dispersion). Our new transect analyses (Fig. R5)
confirm that the crystals are unzoned. We added the EPMA points on the small triangle
on the bottom left of Fig.4a to better show the homogeneity of compositions.
I am also surprised by the fact that according to the modelling there is free garnet in
this sample (Figure 4b), but I am very surprised that garnet compositions are not shown,
because garnet isopleths are very reliable to estimate the PT conditions of
metamorphism.
Response: Garnet exhibits a very homogeneous, Mn-rich composition, with
representative data presented in Table R1 and also complemented by Supplementary
Table S4. Note that the modal proportions of garnet are quite low—0.02% based on
TIMA mapping and 0.25% in the best-fit area of our pseudosection modeling—and thus
exert little impact on the phase relationships. Because of the strong fractionation effect
of garnet (also visible in Table R1), we cannot use the modeled garnet composition for
constraining the peak burial conditions accurately (see for instance Konrad-Schmolke
et al., 2008). Using garnet for constraining peak conditions thus appears a very risky
operation.

use the modeled garnet composition for constraining the peak burial conditions accurately
(see for instance Konrad-Schmolke et al., 2008). Using garnet for constraining peak
conditions thus appears a very risky operation.
Moreover, when building a pseudosection, it is good practice to provide the mineral
chemistry of all minerals in the rock and discuss it to check if it fits or not with the
observed assemblage. This should be done with glaucophane, chlorite, and biotite,
which are expected to be present based on modelling.
Response: It is well known that achieving a perfect fit between modeled minerals and
analyzed phases is extremely difficult, as the solution models are often simplified and
never perfectly replicate actual phase compositions. For instance, the measured X of
Mg

values of 0.64 and 0.97, respectively (see data in Table R1). Glaucophane X value is
Mg
slightly different (0.60 modeled versus 0.72 analyzed), same for garnet (X : 0.12
Mg
modeled vs. 0.17 analyzed). Again, there is not a single study on such a complex system
where a perfect match is achieved between modeled and measured mineral
compositions. A model is never perfect, and the ‘best model’ is the one that most
accurately matches the observed natural system. We believe that we did our best and
cannot converge towards a model more perfectly describing the natural system at stake.
Such considerations might be relevant for a study focused solely on petrology and phase
relationships, but we would like to kindly remind that the core topic of our work is the
documentation and mechanical interpretation of the micro-shear zones. Whether the
micro-shear zone formed at 1 GPa or 1.5 GPa has little to no implication for our
proposed geodynamic and mechanical model. The temperature, which exerts a greater
effect on rheological calculations, is much better constrained thanks to RSCM estimates.
In order to avoid an unnecessary imbalance between pseudosection modelling and
EBSD/microstructures and keep our draft sharp and concise, we prefer to avoid such
technical considerations.

I have also noted that the authors modelled the system in the NCKFMASH system and
do not model nor provide information about Mn, Ti, and Fe2+/Fe3+ (O). This is tricky,
because the presence of Mn could lower the stability of minerals significantly
(stabilizing for instance spessartine garnet at lower T) and Fe2+/Fe3+ affects the stability
of amphibole, garnet, chlorite, and muscovite, and mica isopleths. So why not
measuring and using Mn and O for the modelling?
Response: The point regarding Mn is totally correct: its presence strongly controls the
stability of garnet towards lower temperatures. In fact, MnO was already included as a
component in the grid shown in Fig. 4b; however, we inadvertently omitted it from the
figure caption. This oversight has been corrected in the revised version. Thank you for
raising this matter. The amount of MnO is extremely low, 0.07 wt.% (and was estimated
in the same way as for the other elements). Because of the strong fractionation effect of
garnet (see Konrad-Schmolke et al., 2008, for instance), we cannot use the modeled
garnet composition for constraining the peak burial conditions, as also illustrated in
Table R1.
As for the Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio, we state in the manuscript (Line 425) that phengite, chlorite,
and glaucophane in the vicinity of the micro-shear zone have no ferric iron in their
structural formula (stoichiometric calculations report all iron as ferrous, and in
particular for glaucophane; see Table R1). Given that glaucophane has an Fe3+ end-
member (riebeckite), if oxygen fugacity had been high, this would have resulted in a
significant riebeckite component, which is not supported by the analyzed glaucophane
compositions (Table R1). In addition, the presence of magnetite but the absence of
hematite indicates a moderate oxygen fugacity, below the hematite-magnetite (HM)
buffer. Hence, we are somewhere between the iron-wüstite and HM buffer but
determining accurately the amount of O in the system is extremely challenging and
2
risky. Nevertheless, we have run the model with various Fe2+/Fe3+ ratios and this
invariably leads to the stabilization of aegirine, which is an artefact that is well known
by the metamorphic petrologist community. Since aegirine has not been observed in the
numerous thin sections that have been studied, we conclude that adding O or Fe3+ in
2
our calculations brings an unnecessary level of complexity. We thus prefer to keep
working in a simplified, Fe3+-absent system that more accurately reproduces our natural
system.
I think there is not enough discussion about the limitations of paleopiezometry and flow
laws, which have a large associated uncertainty related to (1) separating recrystallized
grain size and relic grains (Cross et al., 2017), (2) estimating radii from sections without
knowing the 3D shape of grains, and (3) the uncertainty associated with power laws. In
general, it is good practice to try to use different relationships as done by Stipp (2002a,
b) in the Tonale Fault.
Response: These concerns are addressed below one by one:
(1) Separating recrystallized grain and relic grains
The details of separating recrystallized and relic quartz grains follow Cross et al. (2017).
Specifically, we applied the Grain Orientation Spread (GOS) threshold method to
EBSD data to distinguish strain-free recrystallized grains (small grain sizes, low GOS
values) from internally deformed relic grains (larger sizes, high GOS values). Only
fully identified grains—those not intersected by the edges of the mapping area—were
included in the grain size analysis to ensure reliable measurements. In our strongly
deformed sample, the maximum intragranular misorientation of quartz (~15°) is well
above the angular resolution limit of conventional EBSD (nominally ~0.5°), effectively
eliminating the possibility of misclassification due to instrumental limitations.
Although 2D imaging may introduce cutting effects—where fewer than 25% of large
grains are mistakenly identified as small due to sectioning—the measured proportion
of small relic grains in 2D remains statistically representative of their actual proportion
in 3D. Comparisons between 2D and 3D mylonitic microstructure datasets (Berger et
al., 2011) further support this conclusion.
(2) 3D grain shape
The metachert outcrop commonly displays both mylonitic foliation and stretching
lineation (Fig. 1), suggesting that it should be classified as an LS-tectonite—typically
associated with strain conditions approximating plane strain (e.g., K ≈ 1; Flinn, 1962;
Ramsay and Huber, 1987). Finite strain estimations based on Fry analyses of oriented
thin sections from MSMC sample E51 (X–Z and Y–Z planes) yield axial ratios of R
X-Z
= 1.75 and R = 1.32, respectively (Fig. R5a–d). These values further support a near-
Y-Z
plane strain geometry, consistent with L=S tectonites, as shown by the Flinn diagram
(K = 1.03) and Hsü diagram (ν= –0.02; Hsü, 1966; see Fig. R5e–f). In plane strain, the
principal strain axes follow the relationship X > Y = 1 > Z, with extension along X, no
strain along Y, and shortening along Z (Fossen, 2010). Given this 3D strain geometry,
measuring grain size in the X–Z plane would minimize the influence of area distortion
caused by extension and shortening along the principal axes (e.g., Platt et al., 2018;
Tulley et al., 2020; Ujiie et al., 2022). This approach was adopted in our study, as all
EBSD mappings were performed on X–Z plane thin sections, cut perpendicular to the
foliation and parallel to the stretching lineation. Moreover, the primary focus of the
palaeopiezometric analysis—small, strain-free recrystallized quartz grains within the
micro-shear zones—is typically equant in shape, rendering their size measurements
largely insensitive to 2D thin-section orientation.
Fig. R5: Three-dimensional strain ellipsoid shape data from the MSMC sample E51. (a)
synkinematic quartz band in the X-Z thin section from sample E51, with selected grain centroids
(red dots) marked for Fry method analysis. (b) Fry plot of the X-Z planes with red fitted strain
ellipses. (c) Deformed quartz aggregate in the Y-Z thin section of sample E51, showing selected
grain centroids (red dots) used for Fry method analysis. (d) Fry plot on the Y-Z planes with blue
fitted strain ellipses. (e) distribution of MSMC sample (red star) on Flinn diagram (K = 1.03). (f)
sample position (red star) on the Hsü diagram (ν = -0.02).
(3) Multiple flow laws and piezometers
To constrain the uncertainty inherent in flow laws, multiple dislocation-based flow laws
for quartz are plotted in Fig. R6, including: (a) Hirth et al. (2001); (b) the experimental
data of Luan and Paterson (1992), with parameters re-evaluated by Fukuda and Shimizu
(2017); (c) Fukuda et al. (2018); and (d) Tokle et al. (2019).
Fig. R6: Deformation mechanism maps were constructed based on the following flow laws:
(a) Hirth et al. (2001); (b) Luan and Paterson (1992) with parameters redetermined by Fukuda
& Shimizu (2017); (c) Fukuda et al. (2018); (d) Tokle et al. (2019) for dislocation creep, and
Den Brok et al. (1998) for diffusion creep. The boundary between dislocation creep and pressure
solution creep fields shown as a red solid line. Blue dashed line (RG-S&T): recrystallized grain size
piezometer of Stipp and Tullis (2003). White dash-dot-dash line (CG-C): piezometer for coarser-
grained quartz, derived from 1 μm step-size EBSD mapping by Cross et al. (2017). Black solid line
(SR-C): "sliding resolution" piezometer of Cross et al. (2017) as adopted in this study. The semi-
transparent white bands indicate the uncertainty bounds associated with the above-mentioned
piezometers.
As shown in Fig. R6, strain rate variations among the different flow laws applied to our
dataset remain within one order of magnitude and consistently fall within the
dislocation creep regime. Three different piezometers are also included in the
deformation mechanism maps (Fig. R6): the recrystallized grain size piezometer of
Stipp and Tullis (2003); the piezometer for coarser-grained quartz derived from 1 μm
step-size EBSD mapping by Cross et al. (2017); and the ‘sliding resolution’ piezometer
proposed by Cross et al. (2017). The differential stresses calculated using these
piezometers show minimal variation, with discrepancies of less than 10 MPa.
Figs. R5 and R6 are provided as Supplementary Figs. S11 and S9, respectively. The
corresponding explanatory text has been incorporated into the main manuscript (Lines
232 and 438).
It is also necessary to check if the rocks involved where deformed at the same fluid
conditions. For example, if we are in fluid-saturated conditions or not, as this strongly
affects the recrystallization of quartz (Stipp et al., 2006, 2010; Menegon et al., 2011;
Austrheim papers).
Response: The hydrolytic weakening effect in flow strength has been observed for
decades in experiments on quartzites (e.g., Hirth and Tullis, 1992), while exerting little
to no influence on the quartz piezometer relationship (Stipp et al., 2006). Moreover,
further studies have shown that this weakening effect is primarily controlled by the
water fugacity (highly related to confining pressure) rather than by water content alone
(Tullis et al., 1979; Tullis and Yund, 1989; Post et al., 1996). Accordingly, the water
fugacity term ( ) has been incorporated into the power-law constitutive equation for
𝑓𝑓𝐻𝐻2𝑂𝑂
dislocation creep and subsequently extrapolated to crustal deformation conditions
(Kohlstedt et al., 1995; Hirth et al., 2001). In this study, water fugacity is derived under
consistent P–T conditions of rocks (see above) using the equation of state proposed by
Pitzer and Sterner (1994), which provides a thermodynamically robust formulation
valid from near-ambient to upper mantle pressures and is directly fitted to experimental
data. This approach enables accurate and continuous estimation of water fugacity across
the P–T range relevant to both laboratory experiments and natural deformation
conditions, thereby allowing for the reliable incorporation of hydrolytic weakening
effect into quartz flow law calculations.
Case studies of natural rocks have revealed deformation contrasts related to variations
in water and/or melt content, which are typically driven by the following factors: (1)
variations in melt or fluid release associated with metamorphic facies, governed by
contrasts in bulk-rock composition and P–T conditions (Menegon et al., 2011;
Giuntoli et al., 2022; Bukała et al., 2024); (2) infiltration of external fluids along brittle
fractures or shear zones (Austrheim, 1987; Jamtveit et al., 2018). In the studied metachert
block, both the whole-rock composition (high quartz content) and the peak metamorphic
P–T conditions (see above) are notably homogeneous. No evidence of syn-metamorphic
veining with high-pressure minerals, brittle fracturing, or associated bands of hydrous
assemblages has been identified inside the metachert block. Based on these evidences,
we suggest that there was no significant variation in fluid content (pressure and
composition) within the metachert block.
A discrepancy in pore fluid pressure factor (λ) between the calcschist matrix (λ > 0.97)
and the metachert block (λ < 0.86) is concluded from our study (Fig. 5b). Nevertheless,
the consistent activation of quartz slip systems—from rhomb <a> slip to prism <a>
slip—together with subgrain rotation recrystallization (SGR)-dominated dislocation
creep observed in both block and the matrix, suggests that relatively minor difference
in pore fluid pressure (as reflected by a ~0.1 difference in λ) did not exert a significant
influence on the dislocation creep mechanism under consistent P–T conditions. Hence,
we suggest that our piezometric and flow law estimations for both the block and the
matrix remain robust. This is now more explicitly explained in the Flow laws derivation
section of the Supplementary Texts.
Regarding the calcschists, I am also concerned by the fugacity of CO2 and H2O in the
fluid, which may affect calcite and quartz behavior (Pennacchioni paper: Why Calcite
can be stronger than quartz?). Crucially, there are no microphotographs showing the
microstructure of the calcschists
Response: Fair enough. According to the flow law plots of calcite and quartz presented
by Mancktelow and Pennacchioni (2010), calcite is rheologically stronger than quartz
only under the following conditions:
(1) the presence of abundant fluid, such that water significantly reduces the rheological
strength of quartz while having little effect on calcite;
(2) deformation occurs at high to moderate temperatures (greater than 550 °C);
(3) the calcite grains are coarse-grained, with grain sizes on the order of millimeters;
(4) the differential stress is sufficiently low (less than 10 MPa).
In the setting of this study (the transition zone), high water fugacity may exist in the
calcschist; however, conditions (2)–(4) are demonstrably not satisfied. Moreover, as we
mentioned above, both the outcrop (boudinage structures and/or pinch-and-swell
geometries of the quartz veins; Fig 1i) and microstructure (σ-type quartz porphyroclast
within the matrix of the calcite–quartz aggregate; Fig. R3d) indicated that quartz
remained mechanically stronger than calcite during shearing.
Additionally, the corresponding microphotographs depicting the microstructure of the
calcschists are presented in Fig. R3. Nevertheless, we now include additional material
in the supplementary files (Fig. S2 and S7) in order to better show what the calcschist
matrix looks like.
Indeed, the mismatch between paleostress measurements with this approach and
differential stresses measured in modern subduction zones might indicate that there is
an intrinsic error with the method that it is not addressed.
Response: In the block-in-matrix subduction channel setting, numerical modeling
(Kenkmann and Dresen, 1998; Kenkmann, 2000; Ioannidi et al., 2021) has shown that
the integration of stress over the surfaces of relatively rigid blocks can lead to elevated
internal stresses within the blocks. Yamato et al. (2019) have also shown numerically
that indentation of rigid blocks in a weaker matrix can lead to transiently extremely
high stress within touching blocks. In addition, large megathrust ruptures are also
known to be followed by viscoelastic relaxation along the subduction interface that can
persist for several decades (such as for the 1960 Great Chile Earthquake, Wang et al.,
2007), in line with the duration estimated from observed microstructures. Such post-
seismic stress relaxation processes could also have contributed to the generation of the
micro-shear zones observed within the metachert blocks. Notably, the interpretation of
the force-chain-like phenomenon formed by block interactions in this study is also
considered to contribute to the pronounced amplification of internal stress within the
blocks (Beall et al., 2019). These stress amplification effects provide a plausible
explanation for the mismatch between stress values estimated from microscale
palaeopiezometry (tens of MPa; Behr and Platt, 2013; Platt et al., 2018; Tulley et al.,
2020; Ujiie et al., 2022) and those inferred from large-scale geophysical observations
(≤ 1 MPa; Folesky et al., 2024). This concern has been clarified in the manuscript at
Lines 76, 221, 298, 304, 317, and 347.
Finally, the author only discuss one model proposed for the formation of SSE at the
subduction interface, the interaction between strong blocks in a weak matrix, which is
only one of the models proposed. Crucially, they do not provide evidence of interaction
between blocks in their rocks, so why do they focus on this model only when there
could be other explanations related to e.g. fluid activity/fluid overpressure, strain
partitioning, accretion of different blocks with different microfabrics and so on.
Response: We respectfully disagree with this statement. We do not claim to propose a
new model for the formation of SSEs. Rather, the objective of our study is to document
the mechanical effects of block interaction within the region where SSEs are inferred
to occur. It is clear that we cannot document the interaction itself because this block-
block interaction occurred 467 Ma ago, and the former contact zones have been
reworked right after block interaction and later upon exhumation and tectonic
amalgamation during the closure of the oceanic realm. Alternative options, such as
asperity subduction, are now offered in the paper to acknowledge that several
phenomena can lead to the same rock imprint (Lines 320 and 332). We also evoke the
possibility of having post-seismic stress relaxation processes for triggering block
deformation, in addition to deep SSEs (Lines 347 and 350).
Another minor -but important- observation: I do not think it is necessary to stress that
recrystallization is by SGR if you have EBSD data, as when you have those small
micro-shear bands, you need to do a very detailed microstructural work to prove this.
For example, to me, you have both BLG and SGR (Stipp et al., 2002a, b), but it is still
dislocation creep, so it is not important.
Response: Thank you for the kind reminder. As noted above, this issue was also raised
by Reviewer #2 and has been resolved accordingly. While SGR appears to be the
dominant recrystallization mechanism in the micro-shear zones—evidenced by the
shape of newly formed grains and the transition from rhomb <a> slip to prism <a>
slip (Fig. 3 and Fig. S4–5)—we also acknowledge the presence of bulging at the margins of
large grains (BLG). In light of this, we have removed the emphasis on ‘recrystallization
by SGR’ and now refer more broadly to ‘recrystallization by dislocation creep’ in the
manuscript (Lines 224, 251, and 737).
For the reasons stated above, I do not think the data provided in the paper can be easily
tied to the subduction interface or be demonstrated that the quartz microfabrics on
which EBSD was performed were coeval and all representative of deformation at the
plate interface, as most of this may have also been occurred in the exhumation channel
above the plate interface and over a range of PT conditions.
Response: As already discussed above, we prove that we have excellent control over
the place and the timing at which the studied quartz microfabrics formed. It is neither
related to exhumation nor other processes, as already discussed in the discussion section
of the draft. Nevertheless, we have added additional elements in order to clarify these
points in the manuscript.
But the quartz EBSD data shown is of excellent quality and I think the authors can use
it to address issues pertaining to quartz deformation, such as the origin and propagation
of micro shear bands or SC fabrics in a deforming rock (e.g. papers by Trepmann et al.,
Hentschel et al., Finch et al. etc.; Ceccato et al., Kjoll et al., etc.).
Response: Thank you for the constructive comments. Following established EBSD
analytical methods (e.g., Kjøll et al., 2015; Ceccato et al., 2017; Trepmann et al., 2017;
Hentschel et al., 2022), we obtained crystallographic orientations of quartz grains from
different deformation domains (micro-shear zones and coarse-grained ribbons). These
are presented as IPF-X maps with oriented grain shapes, and pole figures color-coded
according to the IPF-X directions of individual data points.
Within the micro-shear zone at the E52-A site, the <c> axis of the host quartz grain is
preferentially oriented subparallel to the Z-axis of the sample's kinematic framework,
accompanied by intense subgrain rotation recrystallization (see bottom left of E52-A in
Fig. R7). These types of host grains, referred to as XZ-type by Ceccato et al. (2017),
are interpreted as having crystallographic orientations that favor early strain hardening,
SGR recrystallization, and the development of micro-shear zones. However, the
comparison between micro-shear zones and coarse-grained ribbons reveals a consistent
pattern in the IPF-X maps and pole figures (E52-B, C71-A, C31-A, and C13-A in Fig.
R7), suggesting rather random crystallographic orientations of quartz. Hence, we infer
that the formation of micro-shear zones was, to some extent, facilitated by the quartz
initial crystallographic orientations with c-axes perpendicular to the Y-axis, as
suggested by Ceccato et al. (2017). Fig. R7 has been included in the Supplementary
Information as Fig. S5, with the corresponding description provided in the EBSD
analysis section of the Supplementary Texts and the Manuscript (Line 158).
Fig. R7: IPF-X maps with overlaid crystal shapes of trigonal quartz, and corresponding IPF-
X color-coded pole figures, from micro-shear zone sites in the micro-sheared metachert metachert.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This is a revised version of the manuscript by Wu et al. I reviewed the original version earlier this year, and recommended publication after minor revisions.
I have looked through the revised version, focusing on the parts of the text that have been revised. I am satisfied that the authors have considered my earlier comments and suggestions carefully, and that they have made appropriate revisions. I have a few corrections of an editorial nature, noted below, but otherwise I am happy to recommend publication.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Dear authors,
I apologize for my late review. I have read with interest the replies to my previous concerns and the revised manuscript and I think many answers are appropriate and satisfactory. The authors did an impressive job in digging through the literature, improving the paper, and providing additional supplementary material that further strengthen the manuscript. I only have minor concerns related to some of the answer and still some more serious concerns regarding the metamorphic assemblage. For this reason, I think minor revisions are still needed before the manuscript can be published.
For the rest, my comments were meant to be mostly though-provoking. I do believe the authors really have excellent EBSD data, Ar/Ar data, and P-T data, but my problem is always: how to correlate a geochronological data that has only +-3 Ma uncertainty (very low in geology) with geophysical data that gathers information about ETS in real time? Same for a rock fabric that is maybe instantaneous in the geological time, but it is the sum of thousands of deformation events.
I do not think the quartz crystal shown in Fig. 3d can be considered a sigma-porphyroclast (or at least it is really difficult to see), but the first part of the response in the rebuttal letter was already satisfactory even without invoking sigma-porphyroclasts. Anyway, I suggest changing the caption or removing this figure.
The response about Mn and Fe2+/Fe3+ is generally satisfactory, but the author state to have calculate stoichiometrically the Fe3+ in chlorite and phengite. Unfortunately, it is not possible to calculate Fe2+/Fe3+ stoichiometrically for minerals that contain more than one partially filled site such as biotite, white mica, chlorite... (see for example Forshaw & Pattison, 2021. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 176:63). Anyway, this can be done for glaucophane and if the authors do not find Fe3+ in glaucophane, and do not have Fe3+-bearing oxides in their samples, then the assumption of all iron to be divalent is correct. Is this the case?
The profile shown for glaucophane (Figure R5n) is not satisfactory, because it only shows the Na content (also according to line 188), whereas Na-amphibole is commonly zoned in Mg, Fe, and Mn. It is necessary to show at least a consistent XMg across the mineral to document that it formed under a single event. In the supplementary, I can only find EPMA chemical data of phengite, and only representative analyses of garnet and glaucophane. ALL chemical analyses should be provided and accessible.
I still do not think the interaction of blocks in the mélange is a suitable explanation for your structures, because you always see them isolated in many mélanges. Their interaction, as proposed by the models cited in your manuscript, leads to clogging, so in their finite strain state you should find them coupled. Other models (e.g. Vannucchi et al., 2022. Nature communications 13, 2311) consider clogging to be physically not possible and argue e.g. for weak blocks in a strong matrix.
I think with your data you could critically consider all these limitations and try to evaluate these models or propose alternatives that fits your data and observation better. Alternatively, why discussing things you have little data about (you have much microstructural data but little field documentation of the blocks, the mélange fabrics and their interaction).
I still do not think all your fabrics to be coeval, because it is hard to tie Ar/Ar ages in mica to quartz microfabrics. One may argue that mica does not recrystallize in shear bands and you may be dating fragments of relic micas disrupted by the shear bands. In any case, I accept the fact that you assume your fabrics to be coeval (as you state in your reply), but I think this should be clearer in the text for the readers. This is crucial, because a slight change in the T of deformation would change the estimation from paleopiezometry and pseudosection modelling also has an intrinsic P-T error of at least +- 1 kbar and +-50 °C, likewise RSCM thermometry.
In general, leaving more space in the text to discuss the limitations of bridging geological data (with its uncertainties) to geophysical data (currently observed SSEs) would make the manuscript more appealing even to non-geologists.
Some minor comments below:
201-202. This is not correct. SGR is not always happening at 420-500 °C. This temperature range derives from the works of Stipp et al. (2002a, b), and these authors stated in multiple works that this temperature range is valid only for the Tonale Fault (this is also reported by Law, 2014). I know that SGR is kinda active around these temperatures but there are conditions at which it might not be, for example at dry conditions (e.g. Menegon et al., 2011). In your case this is irrelevant: you have a pseudosections and other T estimates, so I suggest removing this statement.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-point response to reviewers’ comments for
Nature Communications Manuscript: NCOMMS-25-11434A
Manuscript Title: Stress heterogeneities in exhumed high-pressure rocks shed light
on deep subduction interface transient coupling
Authors: Yawei Wu, Samuel Angiboust, Jianxin Zhang, Bo Zhang, Xiaohong Mao,
Onno Oncken
Dear Reviewers,
We are grateful for your continued and thoughtful evaluation of our revised manuscript,
which has contributed to improving its clarity and robustness. Please find below our
point-by-point responses, shown in blue. Corresponding revisions to the manuscript are
indicated in red where appropriate to address your inquiries.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Thank you for addressing my comments. I am satisfied with the responses and changes,
and recommend publication.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your positive feedback and recommendation for
publication.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This is a revised version of the manuscript by Wu et al. I reviewed the original version
earlier this year, and recommended publication after minor revisions.
I have looked through the revised version, focusing on the parts of the text that have
been revised. I am satisfied that the authors have considered my earlier comments and
suggestions carefully, and that they have made appropriate revisions. I have a few
corrections of an editorial nature, noted below, but otherwise I am happy to recommend
publication.
John Platt, June 3, 2025.
Response: Thanks for your supportive evaluation of our revised manuscript and the
publication recommendation. The editorial suggestions have been addressed as detailed
below.
Line 224. I suggest rewriting the last sentence in this paragraph as follows, for clarity:
“The presence of intragranular Dauphiné twins, which do not cross grain boundaries
(yellow twin boundaries in Fig. 2–3, Supplementary Figs. S3–5), indicate differential
stresses ….”
Response: We appreciate your careful comment and have revised the last sentence of
the paragraph in Line 223 following your suggestion to improve clarity.
Line 229. I suggest “translates to an approximately 600-fold difference in strain rate.”
Response: We replaced “translates to a strain rate difference of approximately 600-fold”
by “translates to an approximately 600-fold difference in strain rate” as suggested (Line
228).
Line 751. I think the rectangle locating part h of Figure 2 is located in part e, not a.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. The error has been corrected, and the text

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Dear authors,
I apologize for my late review. I have read with interest the replies to my previous
concerns and the revised manuscript and I think many answers are appropriate and
satisfactory. The authors did an impressive job in digging through the literature,
improving the paper, and providing additional supplementary material that further
strengthen the manuscript. I only have minor concerns related to some of the answer
and still some more serious concerns regarding the metamorphic assemblage. For this
reason, I think minor revisions are still needed before the manuscript can be published.
For the rest, my comments were meant to be mostly though-provoking. I do believe the
authors really have excellent EBSD data, Ar/Ar data, and P-T data, but my problem is
always: how to correlate a geochronological data that has only +-3 Ma uncertainty
(very low in geology) with geophysical data that gathers information about ETS in real time?
Same for a rock fabric that is maybe instantaneous in the geological time, but it is the
sum of thousands of deformation events.
Response: Thanks for your kind and thoughtful feedback on our previous revision. As
earlier detailed, we utilize an integrated approach combining EBSD-based
microstructural analysis, metamorphic petrology, and geochronology to clearly
demonstrate that the studied blueschist-facies rocks—including metachert blocks and
the surrounding calcschist matrix—were part of, and underwent synchronous
deformation and metamorphism within, the transition zone of the Early Paleozoic North
Qilian paleo-subduction channel. Within this broader framework, the initial cooling
and/or peak metamorphic age of 467 Ma—obtained from our Ar–Ar dating and the Lu–
Hf dating of Cheng et al., (2016), with an uncertainty of ±2–3 Ma—does not
compromise the interpretation that these rocks belonged to, and recorded related
deformation and metamorphism within, this transition zone. In other words, our spatial
and temporal constraints are sufficiently robust to support the aforementioned
interpretation, even though precise absolute timing—down to the scale of years—is not
attainable due to the limitations of current geochronological techniques. More
importantly, while absolute dating at year-scale resolution is not feasible, the relative
duration of micro-shearing events can be indirectly constrained by integrating finite
strain estimates with estimated strain rates, yielding timescales on the order of
approximately 5 to 40 years (see Figure S10 and the ‘Finite Strain Estimation’ section
in the Supplementary Information). Together, these findings enable us to reconstruct a
plausible scenario in which the micro-shearing we observe occurred as a transient event
(lasting several decades) within the ~470–464 Ma timeframe (based on uncertainties of
geochronological data), at a depth of ~55 km in the transition zone of the North Qilian
paleo-subduction channel.
On the other hand, we would like to clarify that we do not propose a direct one-to-one
correlation between the decades-long micro-shearing observed in the block and real-
time slow slip events (SSEs), for the following reasons: (1) there is no direct evidence
of SSEs within the studied block, such as fracturing and/or cataclasis; and (2)
instrumentally detected SSEs typically exhibit rupture lengths ranging from several
kilometers to hundreds of kilometers, with rupture thicknesses of a few meters to
several tens of meters (e.g., Chalumeau et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), which are
significantly larger in scale than the micro-shearing within the blocks we observe.
Rather, we highlight several commonalities in spatial distribution, duration, and strain
rate between the observed micro-shearing recorded in paleo-subduction channels and
modern SSEs observed by geophysical instruments. Given these parallels, we suggest
that the micro-shearing may be related to, or even triggered by, large-scale SSEs (or
post-seismic stress relaxation) occurring in the surrounding faulted matrix network.
Admittedly, this analogy inevitably introduces inherent uncertainties, including the fact
that slow earthquake phenomena arise from a combination of structures and
mechanisms rather than any single controlling factor (Kirkpatrick et al., 2021), and that
the preservation and overprinting of these structures complicate their interpretation in
the geological record (Platt et al., 2024). With this caution in mind, we have elaborated
on these limitations in the manuscript (Lines 346–354) to ensure scientific rigor.
As for the rock fabric, we acknowledge that the observed rock fabric—particularly that
associated with long-term steady-state creep—may indeed represent the cumulation of
multiple (perhaps even thousands of) deformation stages. Nevertheless, our estimated
decades-long duration of micro-shearing constrains the deformation to an exceptionally
well-defined relative timescale (transient in geological time). Even if it’s possible
individual stages remain analytically unresolved, they are nonetheless confined within
the broader geochronological framework established above (~ 467 Ma). Hence, the rock
fabric formed over a certain short time interval should still provide meaningful average
constraints over the whole event, including active slip systems, crystallographic
kinematic frameworks, and flow law estimations. Numerous case studies also
demonstrate that well-preserved and carefully evaluated rock fabrics and structures
could serve as natural snapshots to elucidate the geological mechanisms of slow slip
events in subduction channels (e.g., Behr and Platt, 2013; Fagereng et al., 2014;
Angiboust et al., 2015; Tulley et al., 2020), and even regular earthquakes (e.g.,
Campbell and Menegon, 2019; Papa et al., 2020).
I do not think the quartz crystal shown in Fig. 3d can be considered a sigma-porphyroclast (or at least it is really difficult to see), but the first part of the response in
the rebuttal letter was already satisfactory even without invoking sigma-porphyroclasts.
Anyway, I suggest changing the caption or removing this figure.
Response: Thank you for the meticulous comment. We concur that the quartz domain
shown in Figure R3d cannot be legibly identified as a σ-type porphyroclast.
Accordingly, we have removed the kinematic indicator from the upper right corner and
updated the caption to: “The quartz domain in the center is hosted within a matrix of
calcite and quartz.” as suggested (Fig. S2d of the Supplementary Information).
The response about Mn and Fe2+/Fe3+ is generally satisfactory, but the author state to
have calculate stoichiometrically the Fe3+ in chlorite and phengite. Unfortunately, it is
not possible to calculate Fe2+/Fe3+ stoichiometrically for minerals that contain more
than one partially filled site such as biotite, white mica, chlorite... (see for example
Forshaw & Pattison, 2021. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 176:63). Anyway, this can be done for glaucophane and if the authors do not find Fe3+ in
glaucophane, and do not have Fe3+-bearing oxides in their samples, then the
assumption of all iron to be divalent is correct. Is this the case?
Response: Thanks for the insightful comments regarding the stoichiometric calculation
of Fe2+/Fe3+ of chlorite and phengite. As noted by Forshaw and Pattison (2021), stoichiometric calculations of Fe3+ content are not valid for minerals with more than
one partially occupied crystallographic site, such as biotite, white mica, chlorite, and
staurolite (Schumacher, 1991). This limitation arises from the structural complexity of
these minerals, where multiple partially occupied sites and common vacancies render
charge-balance-based Fe3+ estimates inherently underdetermined and thus unreliable.
Therefore, Fe3+ content in these minerals cannot be accurately resolved from EPMA
analysis alone. In this way, the Fe3+ content of phengite is replaced with ‘—’ instead of
‘0.00’ in Table S5 of the Supplementary Information, to reflect that it cannot be reliably
calculated. Nevertheless, stoichiometric calculations for glaucophane remain valid
(Schumacher, 2007; Hawthorne et al., 2012), indicating that all iron is present as Fe2+
(Table S4). Combined with the absence of Fe3+-bearing minerals (e.g., aegirine) in the
system, we have therefore modeled the system as Fe3+-free, which would more
accurately reflect the natural assemblage.
The profile shown for glaucophane (Figure R5n) is not satisfactory, because it only
shows the Na content (also according to line 188), whereas Na-amphibole is commonly
zoned in Mg, Fe, and Mn. It is necessary to show at least a consistent XMg across the
mineral to document that it formed under a single event. In the supplementary, I can
only find EPMA chemical data of phengite, and only representative analyses of garnet
and glaucophane. ALL chemical analyses should be provided and accessible.
Response: Thank you for this helpful reminder. We agree that including an X profile
Mg
of glaucophane would strengthen the interpretation and better demonstrate its formation
during the peak metamorphic stage. Accordingly, we have updated Figure S7o and its
caption in the Supplementary Information. The revised figure now presents strikingly
flat profiles of both Na p.f.u. and X from core to rim, thereby reinforcing the
Mg
robustness of our interpretation. In addition, we have included the full set of SEM
analytical data for phengite and glaucophane in Table S4 in the Supplementary
Information to ensure transparency and data accessibility. Corresponding revisions
have also been made to the manuscript (Lines 188–189), and all references to the
updated Supplementary Figure number have been corrected throughout the manuscript.
I still do not think the interaction of blocks in the mélange is a suitable explanation for
your structures, because you always see them isolated in many mélanges. Their
interaction, as proposed by the models cited in your manuscript, leads to clogging, so
in their finite strain state you should find them coupled. Other models (e.g.
Vannucchi et al., 2022. Nature communications 13, 2311) consider clogging to be physically not possible and argue e.g. for weak blocks in a strong matrix.
I think with your data you could critically consider all these limitations and try to evaluate these models or propose
alternatives that fits your data and observation better. Alternatively, why discussing
things you have little data about (you have much microstructural data but little field
documentation of the blocks, the mélange fabrics and their interaction).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable and critical perspective. While our
study primarily focuses on the microstructural analysis of individual blocks, we would
like to clarify that it is also informed by systematic field observations of both blocks
and matrix in the Qingshui Gorge mélange (See ‘Geological and structural setting’
section of the Manuscript). These observations constrain their spatial distribution,
geometries, and fabric orientations, as shown in Figure 1 and Table S1, where the blocks
are commonly preserved as isolated, yet closely spaced bodies. In fact, the force chain
model we adopt (Beall et al., 2019a; Ioannidi et al., 2021) does not require that block
interaction leads to sustained jamming or clogging. Instead, their numerical modelling
suggests that force chains composed of randomly distributed clasts after finite shear
strains of about 1, but would subsequently reorganize in response to shear strains of as
little as 0.1 (Beall et al., 2019b). This mechanical instability implies that even if blocks
were transiently coupled with each other at the deep subduction interface during certain
stages of geological history, such block interaction configurations would be inherently
short-lived (transient in geological time), with failure leading to stress redistribution
into the broader matrix and eventual block decoupling. We therefore consider this
mechanism as the plausible explanation for the present-day field observation of isolated,
yet closely spaced blocks in the paleo-subduction mélange.
Alternatively, the strength-inversion model proposed by Vannucchi et al. (2022)
provides a contrasting view. Based on integrated field observations and experimental
data, this model suggests that blocks in subduction mélanges may undergo
hydrothermal alteration and become mechanically weaker than the surrounding matrix.
In such configurations, localized tremor or brittle failure can arise from mechanically
weakened blocks embedded within a relatively stronger, creeping matrix—thereby
circumventing the need for sustained block interaction or clogging. Although the
metachert blocks studied here consist predominantly of quartz, which is relatively inert
during metamorphism and hydrothermal alteration compared to other rock-forming
minerals (Bucher et al., 2002), their rheological strength is nonetheless highly sensitive
to water fugacity (e.g., Austrheim, 1987; Mancktelow and Pennacchioni, 2005;
Menegon et al., 2011; Giuntoli et al., 2022; Bukała et al., 2024). This, coupled with the
inherent mechanical heterogeneity of subduction mélanges, leaves the door open to the
possibility that the blocks may have been locally weaker than the surrounding matrix.
In any case, both the force chain model and the weak-blocks-in-strong-matrix model
allow for transient mechanical coupling and stress transfer within the block-in-matrix
setting. Therefore, we have incorporated the strength-inversion model into the
discussion of manuscript (Lines 316–320), alongside mechanisms such as asperity
subduction (e.g., asperities and seamounts; Moreno et al., 2014) and post-seismic stress
relaxation (e.g., Wang et al., 2007), as potential drivers for the formation of micro-shear
zones within the blocks.
I still do not think all your fabrics to be coeval, because it is hard to tie Ar/Ar ages in
mica to quartz microfabrics. One may argue that mica does not recrystallize in shear
bands and you may be dating fragments of relic micas disrupted by the shear bands. In
any case, I accept the fact that you assume your fabrics to be coeval (as you state in
your reply), but I think this should be clearer in the text for the readers. This is crucial,
because a slight change in the T of deformation would change the estimation from
paleopiezometry and pseudosection modelling also has an intrinsic P-T error of at least
+- 1 kbar and +-50 °C, likewise RSCM thermometry.
Response: Indeed, the dataset presented in our previous revision demonstrates a well-
constrained relationship among quartz CPOs, syn-kinematic mineral compositions, and
both metamorphic and protolith ages in the metachert block and calcschist matrix. On
the basis of this integration, we infer that the quartz microfabrics in both lithologies
formed during a single deformation event, rather than reflecting multiple overprinting
episodes. However, due to the absence of currently developed, datable isotopic systems
in quartz at measurable concentrations, it remains challenging to directly constrain the
absolute timing of deformation from quartz fabrics alone. In light of this limitation, we
acknowledge that our interpretation—that quartz fabrics in both the block and matrix
are coeval—carries a degree of uncertainty. Nonetheless, this uncertainty has been
minimized to an acceptable level through the integration of structural, metamorphic,
and geochronological data. To improve clarity, we have revised the manuscript (Line
239) to explicitly state this interpretation and make transparent the underlying
assumptions.
In general, leaving more space in the text to discuss the limitations of bridging
geological data (with its uncertainties) to geophysical data (currently observed SSEs)
would make the manuscript more appealing even to non-geologists.
Response: We appreciate this constructive suggestion. To broaden the manuscript’s
appeal to a multidisciplinary readership, we have added two concise sentences (Lines
346–353) that summarise both the key limitations and the broader scientific relevance
of linking geological records to present-day SSE observations.
Some minor comments below:
201-202. This is not correct. SGR is not always happening at 420-500 °C. This
temperature range derives from the works of Stipp et al. (2002a, b), and these authors
stated in multiple works that this temperature range is valid only for the Tonale Fault
(this is also reported by Law, 2014). I know that SGR is kinda active around these
temperatures but there are conditions at which it might not be, for example at dry
conditions (e.g. Menegon et al., 2011). In your case this is irrelevant: you have a
pseudosections and other T estimates, so I suggest removing this statement.
Response: As you rightly pointed out, the temperature range commonly associated with
subgrain rotation (SGR) recrystallization (420–500 °C; Stipp et al., 2002a, b) is not
universally applicable. This range was derived from their studies in the Tonale Fault
Zone, and its general applicability is limited, as also indicated by Law (2014), which
noted that SGR activity is sensitive to factors such as water content, strain rate, grain
size, and deformation geometry. Moreover, Menegon et al. (2011) demonstrated that
SGR can be effectively suppressed under dry lower-crustal conditions, even at
temperatures exceeding 500 °C. Given that our study already includes robust
temperature constraints from pseudosection modelling and RSCM geothermometry, we
agree that this general statement is redundant and have removed it from the revised
manuscript (Line 202), as suggested.
