## Methods

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
Thin sections (X–Z plane) were prepared by polishing with the Buehler MasterPrep 0.05-μm alumina polishing suspension and the Buehler EcoMet300-AutoMet300 grinder–polisher, followed by coating with 7.5 nm layers of carbon to reduce charging. Quartz crystallographic orientation mapping was also performed using the FEI Quanta 450 FE-SEM equipped with an Oxford Symmetry S3 EBSD detector in high vacuum mode at the Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences (CAGS), Beijing. The orientation of the thin sections in the analysis chamber was set with the stretching lineation parallel to the SEM X-axis and a tilt angle of 70°. Operating conditions for electron backscatter analysis were: accelerating voltage of 20 kV, beam current of 110–120 μA, step size of 1.5 μm for quartz sheared veins, 0.75–1.0 μm for coarse ribbons, and 0.18–0.9 μm for micro-shear zones. The image collection was completed using the Aztec Crystal software, and data were processed with the open-source toolbox76 for MATLAB (https://mtex-toolbox.github.io/; v. 5.8.1). Grains were defined as areas of a single phase with a misorientation of less than 10°, and the crystallographic vorticity axis (CVA) patterns were determined after77.

TESCAN integrated mineral analyzer (TIMA)
Mineral identification and mica content measurement of coarse-grained metachert (CMC) and micro-sheared metachert (MSMC) thin sections were conducted using the TIMA mineralogy system at the Institute of Geology, CAGS, which comprises a Tescan Mira Schottky field emission scanning electron microscope equipped with four silicon drift energy dispersive (EDS) detectors arranged at 90° intervals around the chamber. The analyses were performed with an accelerating voltage of 25 kV, a beam current of 8 nA, a working distance of 15 mm, and a spot size of 90 nm. The classification of mineral phases and the calculation of their volume ratios were performed by matching the obtained spectroscopic data with built-in mineral definition files.

Electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA)
Mineral chemical compositions of the calcschist matrix and the metachert block were acquired on the JEOL JXA-iHP200F field emission electron probe micro-analyzer at the Institute of Geology, CAGS. An accelerating voltage of 15 kV, a probe current of 20 nA, and a beam diameter of 5 μm were used for acquisitions. Ten oxide compositions were measured with the following standards: SiO2, TiO2, Al2O3, Cr2O3, FeO, MnO, MgO, CaO, Na2O, and K2O. The lines and spectrometer crystals used for the major elements are: Si (Kα, TAP), Ti (Kα, PETJ), Al (Kα, TAP), Cr (Kα, LIFL), Fe (Kα, LIFH), Mn (Kα, LIFH), Mg (Kα, TAPL), Ca (Kα, PETJ), Na (Kα, TAPL), and K (Kα, PETJ). Count times were set to 10 s for the peak and 5 s for the background for each element. Utilizing natural minerals for standardization and performing ZAF corrections yielded an estimated precision of ±2% for major elements.

Raman spectroscopy
Raman spectra of graphite on CMC thin sections were obtained using a Horiba LabRAM HR Evolution spectrometer, coupled with an Olympus BX41 microscope at the Institute of Geology, CAGS. A 532 nm air-cooled frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser was used, delivering 20 mW on the sample with a ×50 objective lens. The scattered light was received by an 1800 gr/mm optical grating through a confocal 100 μm pinhole. After calibration with a silicon standard, we use an acquisition time of 10 s and 2 scans were accumulated within the Raman shift range of 1000 cm-1 to 3500 cm-1. The raw spectral data were fitted using the Voigt function in Fityk 1.3.1 software78. Three peaks, corresponding to the G (1580 cm⁻¹), D1 (1350 cm⁻¹), and D2 (1620 cm⁻¹) bands were identified. Based on the determined peak parameters (Table S2), the quantitative parameter of the graphitization degree (R2 ratio) and related temperature are estimated following40.

Phase equilibria modeling
The major element composition of the MSMC sample E52 was calculated based on the volume fractions of classified mineral phases and their corresponding chemical formulas, which in weight percent is: SiO2 (90.48), Al2O3 (4.13), FeO (1.56), MnO (0.07), MgO (1.31), CaO (0.05), and Na2O (0.69). The phase equilibria modeling of sample E52 was conducted using Perple_X version 6.8.141 and the internal thermodynamic database79 in the MnO-Na2O-CaO-K2O-FeO-MgO-Al2O3-SiO2-H2O (MnNCKFMASH) system. Ferric iron has been neglected in sake of simplicity because analyzed minerals exhibit low ferric iron contents. The a–x relations are provided in the Supporting Information. Mineral abbreviations are given following80. The isopleths of silica content per formula unit in phengite are also constrained in the pseudosection. The comparison between EPMA analyses from the MSMC sample (E52-B site) and modeled mineral compositions (for the best-fit area shown in Fig. 4b), presented in Table S3, reveals minor yet acceptable deviations.

Flow law and slip rate estimation
The EBSD-derived RMS recrystallized grain sizes of quartz (dRMS) were converted into differential stress (σ) using the “sliding resolution” piezometer39, expressed as: dRMS = 104.22 × σ−1.59. The estimated differential stress values were multiplied by 2/√3 to obtain the equivalent shear stress under plane stress conditions46, which was confirmed by the finite strain estimation (Supplementary Fig. S11). The “dislocation creep” flow law from Hirth et al.81 and the derivation details of the deformation mechanism map are included in the Supporting Information.

Assuming the North Qilian paleo-subduction channel underwent down-dip simple shear deformation, the shear strain rate (γ̇) can be expressed in terms of the shear strain (γ) accumulated across an idealized shear width (w), resulting from a finite slip displacement (d) parallel to the subduction interface over a given shearing duration (t). Thus, shear strain (γ) is defined as γ = d/w and the shear strain rate (γ̇) is given by γ̇ = γ/t82. Strain estimates for the micro-sheared metachert range from 0.71 to 2.69, as constrained by syn-kinematic microstructures shown in Supplementary Fig. S10 and the calculation method detailed in the Supporting Information. With constrained strain rates of 10−9 s−1, the process of micro-shearing is estimated to last 5–40 years. Using the relationships described above, the shear strain rate (γ̇) along the subduction interface can be expressed in terms of slip rate (VS = d/t) and idealized shear width (w) as: γ̇ = VS/w.

40Ar–39Ar dating
Syn-kinematic phengite grains were manually selected under a binocular microscope from two crushed blueschist facies calcschist samples (B61 and B62). The phengite grains were ultrasonically cleaned with deionized water and methanol, weighed, placed into aluminum packets, and loaded into quartz vials for irradiation. Irradiation was conducted for 24 hours in the B4 position of the nuclear reactor at the Chinese Institute of Atomic Energy, Beijing, with a neutron flux density of ~2.65 × 1013 n cm−2 s−1. After irradiation, 40Ar–39Ar standard step analyses were performed using a Helix MC mass spectrometer at the Institute of Geology, CAGS. Correction factors for interfering isotopes were calculated during irradiation using irradiated K2SO4 and CaF2. Their values were: (36Ar/37Ar)Ca = 0.0002398, (40Ar/39Ar)K = 0.004782, and (39Ar/37Ar)Ca = 0.000806. All isotopic data are provided in Table S5.

Data availability
The data generated in this study are provided in this published article and its Supplementary Information files.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors argue for the occurrence of deformation at very high shear stresses within an exhumed subduction zone interface melange, at a depth range where stress/strength within the interface is usually considered low. The authors base their argument on structural and micro-structural observations of micro-shear zones. The stress state and strength of the subduction zone interface below the seismogenic zone is an area of ongoing research with implications for understanding the diverse slip styles (slow slip events, tremor, earthquakes) inferred to occur there globally. The authors’ arguments for the high stress state of these micro-shear zones are robust, and will be of interest to a wide range of researchers studying subduction zone mechanics and seismology. I am particularly convinced by how the range of processes throughout the melange are reconciled, such as the contrast in mica content and presence of veins/fluids between the blocks and matrix. I have only one main comment below, regarding the authors’ conclusions about the observed deformation being transient. The main conclusion of the paper regarding localised high stresses is robust and important, even without the point about transience, and I suggest the paper is published after minor revisions addressing this concern.
Main comment:
I am not convinced that there is evidence described in the paper that the micro-shear zones record transient deformation on the time-scale of years. The authors make this hypothesis and therefore relate deformation to slow slip events which occur on similar time-scales (L24, L300, L400). The 1-2 year time-scale is derived in L398 by assuming a strain of ‘at least 0.2 … for quartz dynamic recrystallisation to occur’, such that the years time-scale is a minimum. I do not see an explanation for why the micro-shear zones could not have been deforming on longer geological time-periods. If there is a micro-structural or field constraint on the maximum strain supporting this inference, then the authors should detail this. The formation and breaking of force chains modelled in papers cited by the authors (e.g., Beall et al. 2019) tends to occur at almost an order of magnitude larger strains than described here. The occurrence of slow slip also requires the build-up and release of elastic strain, which is difficult to explain by viscous processes without a sudden loss of strength usually attributed to rapid weakening through fracturing or fluid release/ingress. There is no explanation of rapid weakening in the paper.
Minor comments:
L51 – ‘higher-temperature SSEs’ – It is unclear what this terminology refers to. If you mean SSEs occurring at the base of the seismogenic zone, rather than SSEs occurring up-dip of the seismogenic zone near the trench, then please clarify.
L75 – ‘by 26,35’ – This is a minor stylistic comment that you could include the cited authors names if allowed by the journal as this currently reads awkwardly. This occurs through the paper.

### Reviewer 2

Wu et al
Stress heterogeneities in exhumed high-pressure rocks shed light on deep subduction interface transient coupling
Review for Nature Communications.
General Comments
This paper presents paleopiezometric data from metasedimentary rocks in the North Quilian paleosubduction zone in Tibet. The stress values they obtain from a tectonic block of metachert are significantly higher than those in the surrounding calc-schist matrix, and the authors suggest that this represents transient coupling during slow slip events along the subduction zone interface. The techniques they have applied to determine paleostresses are cutting edge, and their observations, measurements, and calculations all appear to be correct. The interpretation is more speculative; it is interesting and provocative, but it may need some more detailed explanation, and possibly rethinking (see below). Overall, I recommend publication after minor revisions.
My concern with the interpretation is as follows. The authors show that the metachert block has experienced substantially higher stresses and strain rates than the surrounding calc-schist matrix. They suggest that the metachert blocks were relatively strong, and interacted to form force-chains, amplifying the stresses in the blocks for short periods of time (1-2 years). They suggest that this resulted in transient strain-rate events that could correlate with geodetically observed slow slip events in modern subduction zones. My concern is, that if the blocks interacted in this way, the structure of the subduction channel would approximate what is known as the Voigt iso-strain-rate condition, where the blocks protect the matrix from the high stresses, so that the strain-rate in the blocks and matrix are approximately the same. This explains the high stresses in the blocks, but it doesn’t predict high strain rates in the blocks (300 times the strain-rate in the matrix, according to the authors’ calculations). If the strain-rate in the blocks is so high, they can hardly be described as ‘rigid’ as the authors do in this paper. I think the authors need to explain their mechanical model more carefully, or possibly revise it.
Detailed comments
Line 29. “decoupling zone”. This is common terminology among seismologists, but in the context of this paper, it is rather misleading. The zone of ductile shearing below the seismogenic zone involves coupling across the plate interface, in the sense that stress and deformation are transferred across it. The deformation reflects distributed shear, and the lack of seismicity means that there is no evidence of loss of continuity (i.e., slip) across the interface. The authors use “coupling” to refer to this viscous deformation elsewhere in the paper (e.g., line 25). I suggest the authors avoid using this term, as it is ambiguous and misleading.
Lines 112, 647. “thrust folds”. I’m not sure what the authors mean by this. Many folds are related, either directly or indirectly, to thrusting; for example fault propagation folds formed ahead of propagating thrusts, and ramp anticlines formed by thrusting over a ramp. But a fold is not a fault, so I think the term “thrust fold” is a contradiction in terms.
Line 214. Not clear what “these” refers to. May be some text went missing here? The authors appear to be referring to Dauphiné twins.
Lines 220. The difference is stress is about a factor of 4, so with a stress exponent of 4, that gives a difference of strain rate of ~300. That’s large, but not 3 orders of magnitude, as suggested in the text.
Line 289. “Rigid” means the material is so strong that it doesn’t deform. Given that these blocks show very high strain rates, this word does not seem appropriate. Maybe you should say “relatively strong”. But I don’t see how you explain the very high strain rates in the blocks if you propose that they are strong enough to form force-chains. That would mean that the strain-rates should be equal to, or less than, those in the matrix.
Figure 2 (i). There is some discrepancy about grain sizes here. The histograms suggest modes around 10-12 µm for the recrystallized grains and subgrains in B61, which conflict with the values of 55 – 75 µm shown on the plot. The images shown in (a) and (b) suggest that B61 is quite coarse-grained, so it seems the problem is with the histograms. This needs sorting out.
Lines 660-661. The quartz veins are recrystallized by SGR; this is not a deformation mechanism. The deformation mechanism is dislocation creep.
Line 664. Please show or explain what the reference frame is for the CVA plots.
Line 671. The rectangle is in part (e), not part (a).
Figure 3 (d). The resolution in the figure is quite low, and the letters A-A’ and B-B’ are quite illegible in the review copy of the manuscript. Similarly, the plot at the top right of part (d) is completely illegible. In the source file of the figure, these features are visible (if you zoom in a lot). The authors and the production staff will need to work together to make sure the figures are legible in the published version. I would suggest (a) reducing the amount of information in the figure; for example little use is made of the misorientation plot and the MAD plot in the manuscript, and multiple histograms for each sample are not really necessary, and (b) break the figure up into multiple figures so that the individual parts are larger. Much the same is true of Figure 2 and several of the others: they are too “busy” and have too much information in them, not all of which is necessary.
John Platt, March 24, 2025.

### Reviewer 3

This paper is about paleopiezometry in quartz-bearing rocks in an exhumed mélange in China, which is used to document stress heterogeneities in subducted blocks at the plate interface. The paper integrates EBSD mapping of quartz with pseudosection modelling and mica Ar/Ar dating. I have read the paper with interest, I think it is well written, the methodology used up to date, and the quality of the data is good. However, I think the authors make strong assumptions that are never discussed in the manuscript, and there are methodological errors related to the pseudosection modelling and Ar/Ar data. For this reason, I think they need more data to document their model, and to restructure the paper to better address the limitations of their approach. I think a new pseudosection in the MnNCKFMASTHO system is needed, using the chemistry of all the minerals that are available. I also think that they cannot prove the model they propose, about stress heterogeneities along the subduction interface based on this data alone.
First and foremost, the authors use EBSD data from (1) quartz veins in calcschists, (2) metacherts, and (3) micro shear zones in metacherts, and use paleopiezometry and flow laws to estimate differential stress and strain rates from quartz from these rocks. There are two strong assumptions here that are never discussed. First, by analyzing the differential stress recorded by quartz veins in calcschists, it is assumed that those veins registered the same differential stress of the surrounding carbonate-rich matrix, but it is very likely that there was strain partitioning between quartz and calcite, which makes it very difficult to compare this rock with the quartz-rich metacherts. It is like comparing apples and oranges. Second, these microstructures are not necessarily coeval. Micro shear bands may register the latest strain increments in a shear zone, as documented in SC fabrics in the South Armorican shear zone (Berthé et al., 1979; Bukovska et al., 2016).
Second, another strong limitation is that all these rocks were deformed at the same time and that, as such, they register high stresses in the metachert blocks and low stresses in the calcschist matrix, but this assumption is too strong, since the authors could be looking at tectonic slices that were accreted subsequentially from the plate interface and that contain – and this may occur even if the Ar/Ar mica ages from calcschists and metacherts are undistinguishable (Figure S5), because the associated uncertainty of +- 3 Ma does not allow to tell for sure that deformation occurred at the same time (for example, the blocks may have been accreted 1 or 2 Ma after one another). Rapid and subsequent accretion of slices in subduction zones may be expected. There are examples of this from the Sanbagawa belt of Japan for instance (Special volume about Sanbagawa and Ryoke belts on Elements, 2024).
Another strong limitation of this approach is that the Ar/Ar date does not necessarily represent the peak of contact metamorphism, but may represent a cooling age when the blocks were being exhumed together in the subduction channel above the plate interface. In this case, the age is the same because they are dating retrograde metamorphism. This would be consistent with the observation that the closure temperature of mica in the Ar/Ar system (e.g. Harrison et al., 2009) is lower than the peak metamorphism recorded by RSCM thermometry, which is nearly 500 °C (Figure 4).
To better document if deformation occurred at the same time, the authors needs to rely on other dates of peak metamorphism (e.g. Lu/Hf garnet dating, monazite dating) or even to check if the sedimentary age of the different protoliths is similar or very different with U/Pb zircon dating. If the protoliths have very different ages, the authors are likely looking at different blocks affected by retrograde metamorphism above the plate interface.
For the same reason, I have concerns that pseudosection modelling and RSCM thermometry is providing the peak metamorphic temperature. There might be a mismatch between RSCM T, which records the peak metamorphic temperature reached by a sample (which may occur during retrograde metamorphism) and metamorphic assemblage, which may keep the record of the entire PTt path, including the pressure peak. Therefore, it is incorrect to use the best fit between mica isopleths and RSCM temperatures as in Figure b. The measured mica isopleths are stable in most of the pseudosection calculated in Figure 4b, and according to Fig. 4a, there are different generations of white mica. So, why not using these generations to reconstruct a PT path appropriately? I am also surprised by the fact that according to the modelling there is free garnet in this sample (Figure 4b), but I am very surprised that garnet compositions are not shown, because garnet isopleths are very reliable to estimate the PT conditions of metamorphism.
Moreover, when building a pseudosection, it is good practice to provide the mineral chemistry of all minerals in the rock and discuss it to check if it fits or not with the observed assemblage. This should be done with glaucophane, chlorite, and biotite, which are expected to be present based on modelling.
I have also noted that the authors modelled the system in the NCKFMASH system and do not model nor provide information about Mn, Ti, and Fe2+/Fe3+ (O). This is tricky, because the presence of Mn could lower the stability of minerals significantly (stabilizing for instance spessartine garnet at lower T) and Fe2+/Fe3+ affects the stability of amphibole, garnet, chlorite, and muscovite, and mica isopleths. So why not measuring and using Mn and O for the modelling?
I think there is not enough discussion about the limitations of paleopiezometry and flow laws, which have a large associated uncertainty related to (1) separating recrystallized grain size and relic grains (Cross et al., 2017), (2) estimating radii from sections without knowing the 3D shape of grains, and (3) the uncertainty associated with power laws. In general, it is good practice to try to use different relationships as done by Stipp (2002a, b) in the Tonale Fault. It is also necessary to check if the rocks involved where deformed at the same fluid conditions. For example, if we are in fluid-saturated conditions or not, as this strongly affects the recrystallization of quartz (Stipp et al., 2006, 2010; Menegon et al., 2011; Austrheim papers).
Regarding the calcschists, I am also concerned by the fugacity of CO2 and H2O in the fluid, which may affect calcite and quartz behavior (Pennacchioni paper: Why Calcite can be stronger than quartz?). Crucially, there are no microphotographs showing the microstructure of the calcschists. Indeed, the mismatch between paleostress measurements with this approach and differential stresses measured in modern subduction zones might indicate that there is an intrinsic error with the method that it is not addressed.
Finally, the author only discuss one model proposed for the formation of SSE at the subduction interface, the interaction between strong blocks in a weak matrix, which is only one of the models proposed. Crucially, they do not provide evidence of interaction between blocks in their rocks, so why do they focus on this model only when there could be other explanations related to e.g. fluid activity/fluid overpressure, strain partitioning, accretion of different blocks with different microfabrics and so on.
Another minor -but important- observation: I do not think it is necessary to stress that recrystallization is by SGR if you have EBSD data, as when you have those small micro-shear bands, you need to do a very detailed microstructural work to prove this. For example, to me, you have both BLG and SGR (Stipp et al., 2002a, b), but it is still dislocation creep, so it is not important.
For the reasons stated above, I do not think the data provided in the paper can be easily tied to the subduction interface or be demonstrated that the quartz microfabrics on which EBSD was performed were coeval and all representative of deformation at the plate interface, as most of this may have also been occurred in the exhumation channel above the plate interface and over a range of PT conditions.
But the quartz EBSD data shown is of excellent quality and I think the authors can use it to address issues pertaining to quartz deformation, such as the origin and propagation of micro shear bands or SC fabrics in a deforming rock (e.g. papers by Trepmann et al., Hentschel et al., Finch et al. etc.; Ceccato et al., Kjoll et al., etc.).

The occurrence of slow slip also requires the build-up and release of elastic strain,
which is difficult to explain by viscous processes without a sudden loss of strength
usually attributed to rapid weakening through fracturing or fluid release/ingress. There
is no explanation of rapid weakening in the paper.
Response: We appreciate Reviewer #1’s kind comments regarding the potential rapid
weakening mechanisms associated with slow slip events occurring along the deep
subduction channel. However, we would like to clarify that in this study, we do not
directly link the micro-shearing observed in the block to slow slip events (SSEs)
themselves; rather, we suggest that the micro-shearing may be related to, or even
triggered by, large-scale SSEs (or post-seismic stress relaxation) occurring in the
surrounding faulted matrix network. The reasons are as follows: (1) there is no direct
evidence of SSEs within the studied block, such as fracturing and/or cataclasis; (2)
instrumental observations of SSEs have identified rupture lengths ranging from several
kilometers to hundreds of kilometers, with rupture thicknesses of a few meters to
several tens of meters (e.g., Chalumeau et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), which are
far larger than the micro-shearing we observed.
Conversely, we suggest that SSEs, likely accompanied by cataclasis, occurred along
slipping planes within the calcschist matrix, potentially facilitated by rapid weakening,
even though direct evidence for cataclasis is scarce. The trace of cataclasis was probably
erased due to repeated shearing associated with multiple seismic cycles, which led to
the formation of a recrystallized, foliated matrix that has largely overprinted earlier
markers of brittle events associated with rapid weakening (see Kirkpatrick and Rowe,
2013; Oncken et al., 2022; and Angiboust et al., 2024 for further discussion on this
matter). Such velocity-weakening behavior can lead to a loss of cohesion within the
material, ultimately resulting in brittle failure and the release of accumulated elastic
strain (Marone, 1998). High pore fluid pressures in the calcschist matrix could have
played a key role in maintaining the system in a critical state (λ > 0.97, Fig. 5b), close
to rupture. Nearly lithostatic pore fluid pressures are also supported by the presence of
numerous vein sets in the calcschist. We stress that the main point of the paper is not
the report of potential SSE in the matrix but the finding of stress-related micro-shear
zones within the relatively strong metachert blocks. We now better explain in the
manuscript that the concept of having SSEs in the matrix is a hypothesis, which beyond
the fact that it is totally supported by geophysical data, cannot be directly demonstrated
here from the field record (Lines 288 and 347).
Minor comments:

mean SSEs occurring at the base of the seismogenic zone, rather than SSEs occurring
up-dip of the seismogenic zone near the trench, then please clarify.
Response: We indeed refer to SSEs that occur at the base of the seismogenic zone,
rather than those located up-dip near the trench. To clarify this point, we have added
the phrase “occurring at the base of the seismogenic zone,” after “higher-temperature
SSEs” as suggested (Line 53).

through the paper.
Response: We have revised the stylistic issue accordingly by either deleting phrases
such as “has been shown by” or incorporating the cited authors' names where
appropriate, as suggested (Lines 76, 212, and 227).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Wu et al
Stress heterogeneities in exhumed high-pressure rocks shed light on deep subduction
interface transient coupling
Review for Nature Communications.
John Platt, March 24, 2025.
General Comments
This paper presents paleopiezometric data from metasedimentary rocks in the North
Quilian paleosubduction zone in Tibet. The stress values they obtain from a tectonic
block of metachert are significantly higher than those in the surrounding calc-schist
matrix, and the authors suggest that this represents transient coupling during slow slip
events along the subduction zone interface. The techniques they have applied to
determine paleostresses are cutting edge, and their observations, measurements, and
calculations all appear to be correct. The interpretation is more speculative; it is
interesting and provocative, but it may need some more detailed explanation, and
possibly rethinking (see below). Overall, I recommend publication after minor revisions.
My concern with the interpretation is as follows. The authors show that the metachert
block has experienced substantially higher stresses and strain rates than the surrounding
calc-schist matrix. They suggest that the metachert blocks were relatively strong, and
interacted to form force-chains, amplifying the stresses in the blocks for short periods
of time (1-2 years). They suggest that this resulted in transient strain-rate events that
could correlate with geodetically observed slow slip events in modern subduction zones.
My concern is, that if the blocks interacted in this way, the structure of the subduction
channel would approximate what is known as the Voigt iso-strain-rate condition, where
the blocks protect the matrix from the high stresses, so that the strain-rate in the blocks
and matrix are approximately the same. This explains the high stresses in the blocks,
but it doesn’t predict high strain rates in the blocks (300 times the strain-rate in the
matrix, according to the authors’ calculations). If the strain-rate in the blocks is so high,
they can hardly be described as ‘rigid’ as the authors do in this paper. I think the authors
need to explain their mechanical model more carefully, or possibly revise it.
Response: Mixing models for estimating the elastic properties of single-phase
polycrystalline materials have been developed based on the assumption of uniform
strain rate (iso-strain or Voigt bound) or uniform stress (iso-stress or Reuss bound)
(Ioannidi et al., 2021). However, in the significantly more complex natural context of
subduction channel systems, spatial heterogeneity, localized stress concentrations, and
the dynamic evolution of phase connectivity can lead to mechanical behaviors that
deviate substantially from these idealized bounds. The force chain model of block
interactions, as interpreted in the manuscript, suggests that failure of an individual force
chain does not necessarily lead to system-wide stress release (Beall et al., 2019). Instead,
other load-bearing chains remain active and continue to constrain the matrix, thereby
preventing a uniform increase in matrix strain rate. As a result, the overall strain
distribution diverges from that predicted by a Voigt-type iso-strain-rate model.
Previous mechanical studies (Beall et al., 2019; Ioannidi et al., 2021) have shown that
one needs more than 50% of rigid elements to enable the formation of Voigt-type
interaction. At the North Qilian paleo-subduction interface, our field observations (Fig.
1a) indicate that the block content in the mélange is heterogeneous and does not
systematically reach the critical threshold (~50%). This suggests that such localized
force-chain phenomena could not have persisted over prolonged durations, and that the
bulk of the matrix has never been ‘protected’ by the Voigt-type model of hard blocks.
We thus postulate that the low-stress, low-strength portion of the deep subduction
interface matrix that was largely not affected by localized force chain dynamics (the
green strain rate line shown in Fig. 6), which is only visible in metachert, stronger
blocks. The related discussion has been updated in the manuscript (Line 317). The
caption of figure 6 (inset) has been also updated in order to explain that the sketch
depicts the timing of the block interaction and micro-shear zone formation, making
clear that it does not correspond to a steady-state mechanical regime, but rather a
punctual event occurring from time to time when a block-rich segment of the
downgoing crust subducts. In the paper, we now also leave the door open for other
processes, like asperity subduction (e.g., seamount), that may also occasionally locally
impact interface coupling and leave an imprint in the rock record–even though this is
not our preferred option.
Detailed comments
Line 29. “decoupling zone”. This is common terminology among seismologists, but in
the context of this paper, it is rather misleading. The zone of ductile shearing below the
seismogenic zone involves coupling across the plate interface, in the sense that stress and
deformation are transferred across it. The deformation reflects distributed shear, and the
lack of seismicity means that there is no evidence of loss of continuity (i.e., slip) across
the interface. The authors use “coupling” to refer to this viscous deformation elsewhere
in the paper (e.g., line 25). I suggest the authors avoid using this term, as it is ambiguous
and misleading.
Response: Thank you for the meticulous comment. We agree that the term ‘decoupling
zone’, though commonly used in seismology, may be misleading in the context of our
study, as it can imply a lack of mechanical interaction across the deep subduction
interface. In this study, the deep portion of the subduction interface we describe is
characterized by viscous deformation, accompanied by stress transfer and mechanical
coupling that, although reduced compared to the shallower seismogenic zone, still
persists. To avoid this ambiguity and to more accurately reflect the distributed, ductile
shearing behavior observed in this region, we have replaced ‘decoupling zone’ with
‘creeping zone’ in Line 29.
Lines 112, 647. “thrust folds”. I’m not sure what the authors mean by this. Many folds
are related, either directly or indirectly, to thrusting; for example fault propagation folds
formed ahead of propagating thrusts, and ramp anticlines formed by thrusting over a
ramp. But a fold is not a fault, so I think the term “thrust fold” is a contradiction in
terms.
Response: As you rightly pointed out, the term “thrust folds” is not appropriate in this
context. We have replaced “thrust folds” with “thrust-related folds” to more accurately
describe folds that formed synkinematically with thrusting (Lines 114, 726, and Figure
1e).
Line 214. Not clear what “these” refers to. May be some text went missing here? The
authors appear to be referring to Dauphiné twins.
Response: For clarification, we have added “estimates, derived from micro-shear zones”
after “these shear stresses” (Line 221). These stress values remain consistent with the
stress range in which Dauphiné twins form in experimental studies (e.g., Minor et al.,
2018), further supporting the reliability of our stress estimates.
Lines 220. The difference is stress is about a factor of 4, so with a stress exponent of 4,
that gives a difference of strain rate of ~300. That’s large, but not 3 orders of magnitude,
as suggested in the text.
Response: We have replaced ‘strain rates spanning at least three orders of magnitude’
with ‘a strain rate difference of approximately 600-fold’, as suggested (Line 229). The
change in strain rate difference (from ~300 to ~600) stems from reprocessing of the
EBSD data, updated grain size distributions, and a revised estimate of the flow stress
for sample B-61 (see details below).
Line 289. “Rigid” means the material is so strong that it doesn’t deform. Given that
these blocks show very high strain rates, this word does not seem appropriate. Maybe
you should say “relatively strong”. But I don’t see how you explain the very high
strain rates in the blocks if you propose that they are strong enough to form force-chains.
That would mean that the strain-rates should be equal to, or less than, those in the matrix.
Response: Indeed, we have replaced “rigid” with “relatively strong” throughout the
manuscript to better reflect the mechanical properties of the blocks (Lines 309 and 314).
Figure 2 (i). There is some discrepancy about grain sizes here. The histograms suggest
modes around 10-12 µm for the recrystallized grains and subgrains in B61, which
conflict with the values of 55 – 75 µm shown on the plot. The images shown in (a) and
(b) suggest that B61 is quite coarse-grained, so it seems the problem is with the
histograms. This needs sorting out.
Response: We appreciate your helpful comments on the grain size mismatch between
the grain size histograms, their RMS value, and the coarse-grained microstructure
observed in sample B61. Upon closer examination of the EBSD data, we found that this
discrepancy results from pseudo-phase identification during EBSD mapping.
Specifically, under certain orientations, accessory minerals (e.g., phengite) may
produce Kikuchi patterns that partially overlap with those of quartz, leading to pseudo-
symmetric misindexing, where these phases are incorrectly identified as fine-grained
quartz in the raw EBSD data. This phenomenon of pseudo-symmetric mis-indexing is
also reported in the Oxford Instruments technical note (Addressing pseudo-symmetric
mis-indexing in the EBSD analysis of gamma-TiAl - Nanoanalysis - Oxford
Instruments) as well as the EBSD study of natural deformed rock (Dempsey et al., 2011).
This leads to a misleading shift toward smaller grain sizes for the recrystallized grains
and subgrains in the histograms.
To address this, we refined the post-processing workflow for sample B-61 in
AZtecCrystal by first removing grains smaller than 4 pixels, followed by manually
inspecting and batch-removing misindexed, spurious small ‘quartz’ grains located
within phengite domains. For instance, the comparison between the previous version of
the EBSD map, the reprocessed EBSD map, and the corresponding micrograph of the
zoomed-in area in B61-A clearly shows that the misindexed ‘quartz grains’ originating
from the phengite domains have been effectively eliminated (Fig. R2). Following this
post-processing workflow, the EBSD datasets of B61-A and B61-B were reprocessed.
Their EBSD-derived maps, CPO patterns, and grain size histograms have been updated
in Fig. 2 of the manuscript, as well as in Fig. S3 and Table S5 of the Supplementary
Information.
The EBSD-derived maps and CPO patterns remain consistent before and after data
reprocessing. On the other hand, the RMS values of recrystallized grain sizes for
samples B61-A and B61-B increased systematically from 55–76 μm to 100–112 μm, as
expected after the elimination of misindexed small grains, with peak modes typically
centered around 100 μm, in good agreement with the grain size features observed in
oriented photomicrographs. This adjustment in grain size affected the piezometric
estimation, resulting in a slight reduction in the inferred differential stress for sample
B61—from 36–40 MPa to 23–25 MPa. These updated grain sizes and stress values were
also incorporated into the estimation of the flow law and pore fluid pressure factor (λ)
throughout the revised manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper is about paleopiezometry in quartz-bearing rocks in an exhumed mélange in
China, which is used to document stress heterogeneities in subducted blocks at the plate
interface. The paper integrates EBSD mapping of quartz with pseudosection modelling
and mica Ar/Ar dating. I have read the paper with interest, I think it is well written, the
methodology used up to date, and the quality of the data is good. However, I think the
authors make strong assumptions that are never discussed in the manuscript, and there
are methodological errors related to the pseudosection modelling and Ar/Ar data. For
this reason, I think they need more data to document their model, and to restructure the
paper to better address the limitations of their approach. I think a new pseudosection in
the MnNCKFMASTHO system is needed, using the chemistry of all the minerals that
are available. I also think that they cannot prove the model they propose, about stress
heterogeneities along the subduction interface based on this data alone.
Response: Please find our detailed responses below.
First and foremost, the authors use EBSD data from (1) quartz veins in calcschists,
(2) metacherts, and (3) micro shear zones in metacherts, and use paleopiezometry and
flow laws to estimate differential stress and strain rates from quartz from these rocks.
There are two strong assumptions here that are never discussed. First, by analyzing the
differential stress recorded by quartz veins in calcschists, it is assumed that those veins
registered the same differential stress of the surrounding carbonate-rich matrix, but it is
very likely that there was strain partitioning between quartz and calcite, which makes
it very difficult to compare this rock with the quartz-rich metacherts. It is like
comparing apples and oranges.
Response: Thanks for this remark. We have completed our paper with thin section
images of the calcschist matrix (Fig. R3). In Fig. R3, the aggregate of near-equigranular
calcite and quartz grains form a load-bearing framework with a relatively high quartz
content, and where quartz grains are commonly in contact with each other.
Experimental studies have indicated that the strength of calcite–quartz aggregates
increases with increasing quartz grain fraction, reaching a peak at ~20 vol.% quartz
(Rybacki et al., 2003). In the samples studied here, the quartz content of the aggregate
approaches this threshold. Beyond this critical fraction, the bulk rheology of the
aggregates is largely controlled by the mechanical properties of the load-bearing
framework (Handy, 1990), namely quartz. Hence, the microstructures observed suggest
that the strength of the calcschist matrix is mainly controlled by quartz, which would
result in a relatively homogeneous strain distribution without significant strain
partitioning.
In addition, σ-type quartz porphyroclasts within the matrix of the calcite–quartz
aggregate are observed under the microscope (Fig. R3d), along with outcrop-scale
boudinage structures and/or pinch-and-swell geometries of the quartz veins. These
features unambiguously demonstrate that the quartz veins remained mechanically
stronger than the surrounding matrix during shearing.
Given the inapplicability of piezometers to polymineralic aggregates, and the
comparably coarse quartz grain sizes (several hundred micrometers) between the
calcite–quartz aggregates and the quartz shear vein and/or quartz-bearing domain, we
selected the synkinematic quartz shear vein and/or the quartz-bearing domain for EBSD
analysis (B61-A and B61-B). In summary, these microstructural characteristics validate
the application of piezometers to the quartz shear vein and/or the quartz domain as
reliable proxies for the upper bound of whole-rock strength.

Armorican shear zone (Berthé et al., 1979; Bukovská et al., 2016), along with related
literature. These studies demonstrate that S- and C/C′-fabrics formed under distinct
metamorphic conditions—temperatures exceeding 550 °C for the S-fabric, and 300–
350 °C at 100–400 MPa for the C/C′ shear bands. They also suggest that microcracks
may act as precursors to micro-shear bands (see also Fusseis and Handy, 2008).
Following the initiation of early brittle microcracks under high differential stress (up to
creep, accompanied by a marked decrease in differential stress to 17–26 MPa in the
South Armorican shear zone.
In contrast, our data indicate that quartz veins in calcschists and coarse-grained
metacherts, as well as micro-shear zones in metacherts, exhibit consistent kinematics,
as shown by CPO and CVA plots (Figs. 2–3). While we are not certain that the micro-
shear zones represent C-type shear bands, if they do, their formation appears to reflect
kinematic continuity rather than the overprinting of an earlier planar fabric by a later
cleavage, as observed in S–C fabrics from the South Armorican shear zone (e.g.,
Bukovská et al., 2016). Furthermore, syn-kinematic minerals in quartz veins within
calcschists, coarse-grained metacherts, and micro-shear zones consistently formed at
peak metamorphic P–T conditions, without evidence of retrograde overprinting (see
details below). No precursor microfractures are observed in the metacherts, and our
samples lack both macro- and microstructural evidence for polyphase ductile
deformation or retrograde overprinting. In addition, the high differential stress (109–
much lower stress conditions (~10 MPa) reported for late-stage C′ fabrics by Bukovská
et al. (2016).
Taken together, these observations favor an interpretation in which the microstructures
reflect a single deformation event rather than a sequence of overprinting fabrics. The
observed heterogeneities in stress and strain between the micro-sheared metachert and
coarse-grained metachert are best explained by the influence of phyllosilicates (mica)
on deformation and strain localization, in line with both natural and experimental
studies (Tullis and Wenk, 1994; Holyoke and Tullis, 2006; Tokle et al., 2023;
Gottardi et al., 2024).

metacherts are undistinguishable (Figure S5), because the associated uncertainty of +-
example, the blocks may have been accreted 1 or 2 Ma after one another). Rapid and
subsequent accretion of slices in subduction zones may be expected. There are

the ability to conclusively demonstrate synchronous deformation of block and matrix.
However, we still interpret the blueschist-facies unit—characterized by a homogeneous
metamorphic grade within the blueschist facies and composed of these lithologies—as
a snapshot of the transition zone (part of subduction interface) at a specific time (ca.
rock types record the same P–T conditions without evidence of retrograde overprinting
(Fig. R5, see discussion below) and (2) they exhibit comparable deformation patterns,
suggesting kinematic continuity (Fig. 2–3 and S3–5).
In contrast, the eclogite-facies unit represents a deeper portion of the subduction
interface (Fig. 1b) and was juxtaposed with the blueschist-facies unit during late-stage
exhumation (as shown by the observation of localized greenschist-facies mylonites
along the main contact between the two units). The blueschist-facies unit (1.5
GPa/490 °C; Cheng et al., 2016; this study) and the eclogite-facies unit (2.4 GPa/510 °C;
Zhang et al., 2007) represent upper and lower portions of the subduction interface,
respectively, having formed at different depths and possibly at different times. The

facies Shirataki unit formed at different depths along the subduction interface (~55–80
km and ~30–45 km, respectively) and were subsequently juxtaposed during exhumation
(Endo et al., 2024). To conclude, what matters for our study is to demonstrate the
relative coherence of the blueschist facies unit, which is supported by the ages and the
field structures. This is now clearly stated at Lines 99 and 101 in the manuscript.
Another strong limitation of this approach is that the Ar/Ar date does not necessarily
represent the peak of contact metamorphism, but may represent a cooling age when the
blocks were being exhumed together in the subduction channel above the plate interface.
In this case, the age is the same because they are dating retrograde metamorphism. This
would be consistent with the observation that the closure temperature of mica in the
Ar/Ar system (e.g. Harrison et al., 2009) is lower than the peak metamorphism recorded
by RSCM thermometry, which is nearly 500 °C (Figure 4).
To better document if deformation occurred at the same time, the authors needs to rely
on other dates of peak metamorphism (e.g. Lu/Hf garnet dating, monazite dating) or
even to check if the sedimentary age of the different protoliths is similar or very
different with U/Pb zircon dating. If the protoliths have very different ages, the authors
are likely looking at different blocks affected by retrograde metamorphism above the
plate interface.
Response: Indeed, the Ar–Ar age may reflect cooling age rather than the timing of peak
metamorphism, considering that the closure temperature of mica of the Ar–Ar system
(425 ℃ ± 70 ℃; Harrison et al., 2009) is slightly lower than the peak temperature
recorded by RSCM thermometry (~490 °C; Figure 4). Relevant published data also
provide insights into this interpretation. In the Qingshui Gorge blueschist unit, Lu–Hf
isochron dating of garnet, glaucophane, and whole rock yielded a peak metamorphic
age of 467 ± 2 Ma (Fig. R4a; Cheng et al., 2016), which is indistinguishable from our
Ar–Ar mica age of 467 ± 3 Ma. This consistency suggests that the blueschist-facies unit
likely experienced rapid cooling following peak metamorphism. Unfortunately, neither
previous studies nor our work yielded zircon U–Pb metamorphic ages, likely due to the
absence of metamorphic zircon growth. Therefore, based on the available
geochronological constraints, we infer that the peak metamorphic age of the blueschist-
facies unit is ca. 467 Ma, as shown in Fig. 6.
At present, the available constraints on protolith ages come from our unpublished U-
Pb dating results from the Qingshui Gorge, involving two samples related to this
study—a coarse-grained metachert (C13) and the calcschist matrix (B61). Both samples

interpretation is further supported by a maximum sedimentation age of ~511 Ma
obtained from the blueschist-facies unit of the Qingshui Gorge by Cheng et al. (2016),
based on zircon U–Pb analyses. It is worth noting that the presence of a block-in-matrix
structure does not necessarily imply a juxtaposition of rocks with contrasting P–T–t
paths. In the Italian Alps, numerous recent works have demonstrated that units
exhibiting block-in-matrix mixing (that were originally formed as olistostrome basins)
still have strikingly consistent metamorphic trajectories through the eclogite facies (e.g.,
Monviso: Angiboust et al., 2012; Aosta valley: Tartarotti et al., 2017). Therefore,
although the protolith ages of the blueschist facies unit remain partially constrained,
previous studies and our work together demonstrate that this unit consistently records
a well-defined peak metamorphic stage, which provides more robust evidence for
contemporaneous deformation. Same modification of the draft as for the previous

I think there is not enough discussion about the limitations of paleopiezometry and flow
laws, which have a large associated uncertainty related to (1) separating recrystallized
grain size and relic grains (Cross et al., 2017), (2) estimating radii from sections without
knowing the 3D shape of grains, and (3) the uncertainty associated with power laws. In
general, it is good practice to try to use different relationships as done by Stipp (2002a,
b) in the Tonale Fault.
Response: These concerns are addressed below one by one:
(1) Separating recrystallized grain and relic grains
The details of separating recrystallized and relic quartz grains follow Cross et al. (2017).
Specifically, we applied the Grain Orientation Spread (GOS) threshold method to
EBSD data to distinguish strain-free recrystallized grains (small grain sizes, low GOS
values) from internally deformed relic grains (larger sizes, high GOS values). Only
fully identified grains—those not intersected by the edges of the mapping area—were
included in the grain size analysis to ensure reliable measurements. In our strongly
deformed sample, the maximum intragranular misorientation of quartz (~15°) is well
above the angular resolution limit of conventional EBSD (nominally ~0.5°), effectively
eliminating the possibility of misclassification due to instrumental limitations.
Although 2D imaging may introduce cutting effects—where fewer than 25% of large
grains are mistakenly identified as small due to sectioning—the measured proportion
of small relic grains in 2D remains statistically representative of their actual proportion
in 3D. Comparisons between 2D and 3D mylonitic microstructure datasets (Berger et
al., 2011) further support this conclusion.
(2) 3D grain shape
The metachert outcrop commonly displays both mylonitic foliation and stretching
lineation (Fig. 1), suggesting that it should be classified as an LS-tectonite—typically
associated with strain conditions approximating plane strain (e.g., K ≈ 1; Flinn, 1962;
Ramsay and Huber, 1987). Finite strain estimations based on Fry analyses of oriented
thin sections from MSMC sample E51 (X–Z and Y–Z planes) yield axial ratios of R
X-Z
= 1.75 and R = 1.32, respectively (Fig. R5a–d). These values further support a near-
Y-Z
plane strain geometry, consistent with L=S tectonites, as shown by the Flinn diagram
(K = 1.03) and Hsü diagram (ν= –0.02; Hsü, 1966; see Fig. R5e–f). In plane strain, the
principal strain axes follow the relationship X > Y = 1 > Z, with extension along X, no
strain along Y, and shortening along Z (Fossen, 2010). Given this 3D strain geometry,
measuring grain size in the X–Z plane would minimize the influence of area distortion
caused by extension and shortening along the principal axes (e.g., Platt et al., 2018;
Tulley et al., 2020; Ujiie et al., 2022). This approach was adopted in our study, as all
EBSD mappings were performed on X–Z plane thin sections, cut perpendicular to the
foliation and parallel to the stretching lineation. Moreover, the primary focus of the
palaeopiezometric analysis—small, strain-free recrystallized quartz grains within the
micro-shear zones—is typically equant in shape, rendering their size measurements
largely insensitive to 2D thin-section orientation.

It is also necessary to check if the rocks involved where deformed at the same fluid
conditions. For example, if we are in fluid-saturated conditions or not, as this strongly
affects the recrystallization of quartz (Stipp et al., 2006, 2010; Menegon et al., 2011;
Austrheim papers).
Response: The hydrolytic weakening effect in flow strength has been observed for
decades in experiments on quartzites (e.g., Hirth and Tullis, 1992), while exerting little
to no influence on the quartz piezometer relationship (Stipp et al., 2006). Moreover,
further studies have shown that this weakening effect is primarily controlled by the
water fugacity (highly related to confining pressure) rather than by water content alone
(Tullis et al., 1979; Tullis and Yund, 1989; Post et al., 1996). Accordingly, the water
fugacity term ( ) has been incorporated into the power-law constitutive equation for
𝑓𝑓𝐻𝐻2𝑂𝑂
dislocation creep and subsequently extrapolated to crustal deformation conditions
(Kohlstedt et al., 1995; Hirth et al., 2001). In this study, water fugacity is derived under
consistent P–T conditions of rocks (see above) using the equation of state proposed by
Pitzer and Sterner (1994), which provides a thermodynamically robust formulation
valid from near-ambient to upper mantle pressures and is directly fitted to experimental
data. This approach enables accurate and continuous estimation of water fugacity across
the P–T range relevant to both laboratory experiments and natural deformation
conditions, thereby allowing for the reliable incorporation of hydrolytic weakening
effect into quartz flow law calculations.
Case studies of natural rocks have revealed deformation contrasts related to variations
in water and/or melt content, which are typically driven by the following factors: (1)
variations in melt or fluid release associated with metamorphic facies, governed by
contrasts in bulk-rock composition and P–T conditions (Menegon et al., 2011;
Giuntoli et al., 2022; Bukała et al., 2024); (2) infiltration of external fluids along brittle
fractures or shear zones (Austrheim, 1987; Jamtveit et al., 2018). In the studied metachert
block, both the whole-rock composition (high quartz content) and the peak metamorphic
P–T conditions (see above) are notably homogeneous. No evidence of syn-metamorphic
veining with high-pressure minerals, brittle fracturing, or associated bands of hydrous
assemblages has been identified inside the metachert block. Based on these evidences,
we suggest that there was no significant variation in fluid content (pressure and
composition) within the metachert block.
A discrepancy in pore fluid pressure factor (λ) between the calcschist matrix (λ > 0.97)
and the metachert block (λ < 0.86) is concluded from our study (Fig. 5b). Nevertheless,
the consistent activation of quartz slip systems—from rhomb <a> slip to prism <a>
slip—together with subgrain rotation recrystallization (SGR)-dominated dislocation
creep observed in both block and the matrix, suggests that relatively minor difference
in pore fluid pressure (as reflected by a ~0.1 difference in λ) did not exert a significant
influence on the dislocation creep mechanism under consistent P–T conditions. Hence,
we suggest that our piezometric and flow law estimations for both the block and the
matrix remain robust. This is now more explicitly explained in the Flow laws derivation
section of the Supplementary Texts.

Response: Fair enough. According to the flow law plots of calcite and quartz presented
by Mancktelow and Pennacchioni (2010), calcite is rheologically stronger than quartz
only under the following conditions:
(1) the presence of abundant fluid, such that water significantly reduces the rheological
strength of quartz while having little effect on calcite;
(2) deformation occurs at high to moderate temperatures (greater than 550 °C);
(3) the calcite grains are coarse-grained, with grain sizes on the order of millimeters;
(4) the differential stress is sufficiently low (less than 10 MPa).
In the setting of this study (the transition zone), high water fugacity may exist in the
calcschist; however, conditions (2)–(4) are demonstrably not satisfied. Moreover, as we
mentioned above, both the outcrop (boudinage structures and/or pinch-and-swell
geometries of the quartz veins; Fig 1i) and microstructure (σ-type quartz porphyroclast
within the matrix of the calcite–quartz aggregate; Fig. R3d) indicated that quartz
remained mechanically stronger than calcite during shearing.
Additionally, the corresponding microphotographs depicting the microstructure of the
calcschists are presented in Fig. R3. Nevertheless, we now include additional material
in the supplementary files (Fig. S2 and S7) in order to better show what the calcschist
matrix looks like.
Indeed, the mismatch between paleostress measurements with this approach and
differential stresses measured in modern subduction zones might indicate that there is
an intrinsic error with the method that it is not addressed.
Response: In the block-in-matrix subduction channel setting, numerical modeling
(Kenkmann and Dresen, 1998; Kenkmann, 2000; Ioannidi et al., 2021) has shown that
the integration of stress over the surfaces of relatively rigid blocks can lead to elevated
internal stresses within the blocks. Yamato et al. (2019) have also shown numerically
that indentation of rigid blocks in a weaker matrix can lead to transiently extremely
high stress within touching blocks. In addition, large megathrust ruptures are also
known to be followed by viscoelastic relaxation along the subduction interface that can
persist for several decades (such as for the 1960 Great Chile Earthquake, Wang et al.,
2007), in line with the duration estimated from observed microstructures. Such post-
seismic stress relaxation processes could also have contributed to the generation of the
micro-shear zones observed within the metachert blocks. Notably, the interpretation of
the force-chain-like phenomenon formed by block interactions in this study is also
considered to contribute to the pronounced amplification of internal stress within the
blocks (Beall et al., 2019). These stress amplification effects provide a plausible
explanation for the mismatch between stress values estimated from microscale
palaeopiezometry (tens of MPa; Behr and Platt, 2013; Platt et al., 2018; Tulley et al.,
2020; Ujiie et al., 2022) and those inferred from large-scale geophysical observations
(≤ 1 MPa; Folesky et al., 2024). This concern has been clarified in the manuscript at
Lines 76, 221, 298, 304, 317, and 347.
Finally, the author only discuss one model proposed for the formation of SSE at the
subduction interface, the interaction between strong blocks in a weak matrix, which is
only one of the models proposed. Crucially, they do not provide evidence of interaction
between blocks in their rocks, so why do they focus on this model only when there
could be other explanations related to e.g. fluid activity/fluid overpressure, strain
partitioning, accretion of different blocks with different microfabrics and so on.
Response: We respectfully disagree with this statement. We do not claim to propose a
new model for the formation of SSEs. Rather, the objective of our study is to document
the mechanical effects of block interaction within the region where SSEs are inferred
to occur. It is clear that we cannot document the interaction itself because this block-
block interaction occurred 467 Ma ago, and the former contact zones have been
reworked right after block interaction and later upon exhumation and tectonic
amalgamation during the closure of the oceanic realm. Alternative options, such as
asperity subduction, are now offered in the paper to acknowledge that several
phenomena can lead to the same rock imprint (Lines 320 and 332). We also evoke the
possibility of having post-seismic stress relaxation processes for triggering block
deformation, in addition to deep SSEs (Lines 347 and 350).
Another minor -but important- observation: I do not think it is necessary to stress that
recrystallization is by SGR if you have EBSD data, as when you have those small
micro-shear bands, you need to do a very detailed microstructural work to prove this.
For example, to me, you have both BLG and SGR (Stipp et al., 2002a, b), but it is still
dislocation creep, so it is not important.
Response: Thank you for the kind reminder. As noted above, this issue was also raised
by Reviewer #2 and has been resolved accordingly. While SGR appears to be the
dominant recrystallization mechanism in the micro-shear zones—evidenced by the
shape of newly formed grains and the transition from rhomb <a> slip to prism <a>
slip (Fig. 3 and Fig. S4–5)—we also acknowledge the presence of bulging at the margins of
large grains (BLG). In light of this, we have removed the emphasis on ‘recrystallization
by SGR’ and now refer more broadly to ‘recrystallization by dislocation creep’ in the
manuscript (Lines 224, 251, and 737).
For the reasons stated above, I do not think the data provided in the paper can be easily
tied to the subduction interface or be demonstrated that the quartz microfabrics on
which EBSD was performed were coeval and all representative of deformation at the
plate interface, as most of this may have also been occurred in the exhumation channel
above the plate interface and over a range of PT conditions.
Response: As already discussed above, we prove that we have excellent control over
the place and the timing at which the studied quartz microfabrics formed. It is neither
related to exhumation nor other processes, as already discussed in the discussion section
of the draft. Nevertheless, we have added additional elements in order to clarify these
points in the manuscript.
But the quartz EBSD data shown is of excellent quality and I think the authors can use
it to address issues pertaining to quartz deformation, such as the origin and propagation
of micro shear bands or SC fabrics in a deforming rock (e.g. papers by Trepmann et al.,
Hentschel et al., Finch et al. etc.; Ceccato et al., Kjoll et al., etc.).
Response: Thank you for the constructive comments. Following established EBSD
analytical methods (e.g., Kjøll et al., 2015; Ceccato et al., 2017; Trepmann et al., 2017;
Hentschel et al., 2022), we obtained crystallographic orientations of quartz grains from
different deformation domains (micro-shear zones and coarse-grained ribbons). These
are presented as IPF-X maps with oriented grain shapes, and pole figures color-coded
according to the IPF-X directions of individual data points.
Within the micro-shear zone at the E52-A site, the <c> axis of the host quartz grain is
preferentially oriented subparallel to the Z-axis of the sample's kinematic framework,
accompanied by intense subgrain rotation recrystallization (see bottom left of E52-A in
Fig. R7). These types of host grains, referred to as XZ-type by Ceccato et al. (2017),
are interpreted as having crystallographic orientations that favor early strain hardening,
SGR recrystallization, and the development of micro-shear zones. However, the
comparison between micro-shear zones and coarse-grained ribbons reveals a consistent
pattern in the IPF-X maps and pole figures (E52-B, C71-A, C31-A, and C13-A in Fig.
R7), suggesting rather random crystallographic orientations of quartz. Hence, we infer
that the formation of micro-shear zones was, to some extent, facilitated by the quartz
initial crystallographic orientations with c-axes perpendicular to the Y-axis, as
suggested by Ceccato et al. (2017). Fig. R7 has been included in the Supplementary
Information as Fig. S5, with the corresponding description provided in the EBSD
analysis section of the Supplementary Texts and the Manuscript (Line 158).
